extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers revising drafts (and their editors/instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical, chapter-by-chapter editing checklist for fiction writers to use when revising prose, scenes, dialogue, point of view, pacing, and voice. Designed to help an author systematically find and fix common craft problems in a draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show and Tell
rubrics_metrics.description: The classic 'show, don't tell' — but more nuanced. Showing should dominate scenes; telling has its place for transitions and summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use showing (action, sensory detail, behavior) to dramatize scenes; reserve telling for necessary connective material and concise summaries. Avoid showing followed immediately by explanatory telling that restates what the scene already conveyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and Exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid info-dumps about character history. Characterization should emerge over the story through action, dialogue, and reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal character through what they do and say rather than long expository passages. Integrate necessary background in small doses tied to present action so exposition doesn't interrupt narrative flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of View
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose POV deliberately (first, third limited, omniscient); don't head-hop within a scene; use POV to control reader access to interiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent focal character within scenes; decide how much interior thought the POV affords and avoid unauthorized omniscience. Use POV choices to shape what the reader knows and experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Pace by expanding important scenes and summarizing minor ones; the proportion of pages devoted to a scene signals its importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate page/paragraph length to reflect a scene's narrative weight. Lengthening major scenes and compressing incidental events clarifies emphasis and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue Mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'said' almost exclusively as a dialogue tag; replace many tags with action beats; never use adverb-loaded tags; let dialogue carry tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer silent 'said' or action beats over flashy synonyms (avoid 'stated,' 'exclaimed,' 'ejaculated'). Do not qualify 'said' with adverbs like 'she said angrily' — show anger in the dialogue or beats instead. Use action beats to identify speakers, reveal character, and control pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: See How It Sounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your work aloud. The ear catches what the eye misses — clunky rhythm, repeated words, dead phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vocalization as an editing tool to detect awkward sentence rhythm, repeated diction, unnatural dialogue, and phrasing that looks okay on the page but reads poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior Monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: Use interior monologue. Novels can move freely between action and thought to provide interiority that visual media often lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow appropriate access to a character's thoughts to deepen characterization or clarify motivation, but integrate thought with action and avoid over-explaining or halting the scene's forward motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy Beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Action beats (small physical actions) carry dialogue better than tags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use beats to reveal character via gesture, control pacing, establish setting silently, and identify the speaker. Favor unobtrusive physical detail over heavy tagging to keep scenes grounded and dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking Up Is Easy to Do
rubrics_metrics.description: Long passages of any kind (dialogue, description, exposition) need breaking up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shorter paragraphs and breaks to let the reader breathe and to maintain momentum. Avoid extended uninterrupted blocks of text that can feel dense and slow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Once Is Usually Enough
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't repeat for emphasis. Don't restate the same point in different words. Trust the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundancy and repeated explanation of what a scene has already shown. Remove duplicate signals and let inference do work for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid clichés, sentence-level redundancy, explicit statements of emotion when it can be shown, moralizing, and author intrusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for fresh language and subtlety; eliminate dead phrases and unnecessary statements of feeling or judgment. Keep the author's presence out of the narrative voice unless deliberate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice is the cumulative imprint of all the above choices. It is what's left when you take away all the techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop voice by applying craft choices consistently; voice cannot be added on top of weak technique — it is uncovered through disciplined revision and attention to the other principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: R.U.E. — Resist the Urge to Explain
rubrics_metrics.description: After showing, do not then tell. After telling once, do not tell again. Don't explain motivations the dialogue made clear. Don't gloss what the action already showed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use restraint: eliminate explanatory sentences that restate what has been dramatized. Let implications stand rather than over-clarifying for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative Use — Common problems detected
rubrics_metrics.description: A draft can be checked against each principle to locate frequent failings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for typical errors when self-editing: adverb-laden tags; telling after showing; head-hopping within scenes; disproportionate scene length; clichés and dead phrases; exposition lumps. Use the twelve principles as a checklist to find and correct these issues.
